stages.title: The Theory
body: Products and services
What does a hospitality business offer, and what do people do for customers?
Point, say, sort or write.
stages.notes: Untimed. Link to Week 1 business and role work. Explain the two linked questions: what is on offer and what someone does for a customer. stages.title: Arrival task
body: Name two hospitality businesses.
What does service mean?
There is a spill on the floor. What do you do first?
Does a hotel only sell rooms?
BLUE / GREEN / AMBER / RED. Pause, breathe or choose a quieter seat.
stages.notes: 4 minutes. BLUE low energy; GREEN ready; AMBER tense; RED overwhelmed. Offer water, quiet breathing, a brief pause or a quieter seat without requiring a public colour disclosure. Privately agree one return action. Expected: any two appropriate hospitality businesses; an action done for a customer; stop, keep clear, alert the adult and follow the safe clean-up instructions; no, a hotel may offer food and other products or services. This is a discussion, not a spill-handling activity. Individual stations; no pair work or cold calling. Adults may read, rephrase or scribe exact learner words and record support. They do not choose the learner’s assessed sort, labels or explanation. Only VF, WS, I, NS, E and R are used; confirm local code definitions before marking. Blank templates and copied models are not completed individual evidence.

stages.title: A café visit
body: Think about a café, or use the model example.
You buy a sandwich. Someone takes your order.
Which is the product? Which is the service?
The __ is a product. __ is a service.
stages.notes: 2 minutes. The source asks about a past café visit, but learners need not disclose or have visited one. Model answer: sandwich is the product; taking the order is a service. A single purchase can include both. Accept pointing to the relevant card or a short answer.

stages.title: Today I can
body: Sort hospitality items into products and services and explain the difference.
I can sort an item or an action.
I can explain one choice.
I can plan my display.
stages.notes: Untimed. Read the exact supplied outcome. [QUAL] — planner mapping. The short I-can statements are classroom success checks, not quotations from the official student book. The room-offer clarification is recorded in source notes and ERRATA.

stages.title: Product or service
body: Products: sandwich, room offer, coffee, cake.
Services: welcome, cleaning, booking, delivery.
Holding an item is a clue, not a rule.
A hotel room offer also comes with services.
I chose __ because __.
stages.notes: 5 minutes. Model the eight source examples. A product is an item or offer a customer can buy; a service is an action done for a customer. The workbook teaches room as a product but suggests “can you hold it?” as the test. This lesson keeps the room as a bookable hotel offer sold to a guest, with booking and cleaning as services. Holding is a clue for many physical products, not a defining rule. A room/stay combines an offer and services. Accept a well-reasoned alternative classification and record the reason; do not mark a learner wrong merely for noticing the mixed offer. Ask the hinge: “I cannot hold a hotel room, so it cannot be the hotel’s product.” Expected: the holding clue has exceptions; the hotel sells a room offer and provides services around it.

visual.caption: Holding an item is a clue, not a rule.

stages.title: Sort and explain together
body: Sort: packed lunch, booking a room, bottled water, clearing a table.
Name the business for two choices.
The __ is a product because __.
__ is a service because __.
stages.notes: 5 minutes. Expected: packed lunch and bottled water are products; booking a room and clearing a table are services. Link at least two to a relevant business: event catering, hotel or café. Learners point, say or write; no pair work. Check the sort before learners start their own display plan. If someone notices mixed products and services in a package, ask for their reason rather than treating the distinction as universal.

stages.title: Your sixteen card sort
body: Sort sixteen cards across café, hotel and event catering.
Use product or service. Explain one choice.
Supported: use a smaller set first, then add the rest.
Independent: sort all sixteen and add an example.
Aspire: explain a product that comes with a service.
stages.notes: 12 minutes. First part of the 18-minute individual task. Use the numbered sixteen-card bank and evidence record. The Supported route may start in smaller chunks; record what was actually completed. The MCQ support has exactly two misplaced cards to find: coffee is placed as a service and cleaning a room as a product. Do not describe that route as an independent full sort. Adult checks the learner’s sort before the display plan. Individual stations; no pair work or cold calling. Adults may read, rephrase or scribe exact learner words and record support. They do not choose the learner’s assessed sort, labels or explanation. Only VF, WS, I, NS, E and R are used; confirm local code definitions before marking. Blank templates and copied models are not completed individual evidence.

route_tasks.Supported: Chunk the cards; point, match or dictate. MCQ: find two errors in the model sort.
route_tasks.Independent: Sort all sixteen and add an accurate item of your own.
route_tasks.Aspire: Explain a mixed offer, such as room offer plus housekeeping.

stages.title: Your display plan
body: Choose at least two business types for your display.
Plan products, services and clear labels.
My display will show __ and __.
Supported: choose from the labelled cards.
Independent: record your own plan.
Aspire: explain how the layout helps the reader.
stages.notes: 6 minutes. Completes the 18-minute You Do. VOC2-L1-E1 is the learner’s sort; VOC2-L1-E2 is the plan. The next lesson asks for at least four products, four services, two business types and every item labelled; use those as the plan target. These are workbook classroom success checks, not asserted official wording. Learners choose their own items, with card access if needed.

route_tasks.Supported: Choose businesses and items from the cards; dictate your plan.
route_tasks.Independent: Plan four products and four services across at least two businesses.
route_tasks.Aspire: Explain how your layout will make the categories clear.

stages.title: Tidy and check
body: File your sort and display plan.
Check that your plan includes both products and services.
Keep your own reason with your sort.
I still need to __.
stages.notes: 4 minutes. Tidy the station and file the two evidence items. Use the evidence app only under the approved workflow; do not invent file references or capture records. Leave actual date, duration and initials blank until taught. Record the learner’s support, especially a reduced-card or two-error MCQ route. Record actual hospitality participation under the workbook’s agreed-Plan rule; no attendance credit or Careers minutes.

stages.title: Exit ticket
body: Name one hotel product and one hotel service.
Explain one of your choices.
The hotel offers __. A service is __.
stages.notes: 2 minutes. Private check-in, written answer or pointing. Workbook-convention example: room offer or breakfast as the product; booking or room cleaning as a service. Accept a defensible different room/stay classification if the learner explains the mixed offer. Use the answer to identify a single next step.

stages.title: Key words
body: Product: an item or offer a customer can buy.
Service: an action done for a customer.
Menu: food and drink on offer.
Brochure: a small information booklet.
Range: variety.
Display: information arranged for others to see.
stages.notes: Untimed reference. Read the short meanings and use the labelled examples. The product/service distinction in this lesson follows the workbook convention for a room offer. Colour is never the only category cue; use words, pictures and item numbers.

support_pages.title: Sixteen sorting cards
lines: Cut apart or point. Keep the number and business label with each item. Sort each one as product or service.

support_pages.title: Product and service prompts
lines: Product: an item or offer the customer can buy. Service: an action done for the customer.
A sandwich is a product; taking the order is a service. A hotel room offer is the product in this workbook; booking and cleaning are services around it.
Can you hold it? This can help with food and drink, but it is not a rule for every offer. Explain your choice if an example includes both.
Frames: I put __ under __ because __. The __ business offers __.
Supported: sort a smaller group first, then add cards. Independent: complete the set. Aspire: explain an offer that includes services.

support_pages.title: Find two errors
lines: This is a support model, not your completed independent sort. Two cards are in the wrong category. Find them and explain the correction.
Products: 1 sandwich; 3 cake; 7 room offer; 8 breakfast; 10 cleaning a room; 12 packed lunch; 13 bottled water; 14 fruit cup.
Services: 2 coffee; 4 welcoming a customer; 5 taking an order; 6 clearing a table; 9 booking a room; 11 helping with luggage; 15 delivering food; 16 serving food.
I would move card __ to __ because __.

evidence_pages.title: My products and services sort
instructions: Record your own sort of the sixteen numbered cards. Use P for product or S for service, then explain one choice.
A room/stay may combine an offer and services. If you classify it differently, give your reason.
fields: My reason: I put __________ under __________ because __________
My room offer reason if needed: ____________________________

evidence_pages.title: My display plan
instructions: Choose at least two business types. Plan a display with four products, four services and clear labels.
You choose the layout. Use pictures or cut outs from the supplied materials.

staff_answers: The sixteen-card bank contains eight products and eight services using the workbook convention. Products: 1 sandwich, 2 coffee, 3 cake, 7 room offer, 8 breakfast, 12 packed lunch, 13 bottled water and 14 fruit cup. Services: 4 welcoming, 5 taking an order, 6 clearing a table, 9 booking a room, 10 cleaning a room, 11 helping with luggage, 15 delivering food and 16 serving food.

MCQ support model: card 2 coffee belongs with products; card 10 cleaning a room belongs with services. Ask for the learner’s own reason and record support. The model must not be filed as if the learner independently sorted all sixteen.

Room-offer nuance: keep the workbook convention clear, but accept a reasoned alternative account of accommodation as a service or a mixed offer. Do not use “can you hold it?” as a universal definition.

A strong plan names at least two businesses, considers both product and service examples and plans clear labels. The next lesson’s classroom checks are four products, four services, two business types and every item labelled.

Exit examples: room offer or breakfast; booking, cleaning or luggage help. Accept defensible alternatives with an explanation. Record actual ownership, support and minutes; do not assert official completion from classroom examples.
cutout_instructions: Cut apart or point to one card at a time. Keep the card number, business type and item or action together.
Sort all sixteen cards as product or service. Give your own reason for an ambiguous mixed offer.

Lundy Space: individual station. Voice: learner chooses categories and display items. Audience: adult listens to the explanation. Influence: the learner can revise a category or clarify the plan after feedback.

planner_sections.heading: Filing and minutes
paragraphs: Planned hospitality time is 40 minutes. Actual active minutes, date, evidence reference, support and adult initials remain blank until taught. Follow the supplied workbook’s agreed-Plan rule and count real activity only. Careers contributes no hospitality minutes.
File the learner’s own sort and plan in the approved workflow using the evidence app. A planner mapping is not an automatic completed challenge or certification claim.

minutes_record.policy: Record actual eligible work after the agreed Plan. Do not infer time or completed evidence from a blank template.
